one_liner: Research fork of picoquic that swaps kernel UDP sockets for DPDK; about 3x picoquic single-connection goodput on 100 GbE.
what_it_does: A patched copy of the picoquic C QUIC stack (picoquic v1.01 era) whose socket loop is replaced by a DPDK poll-mode loop, plus a minimal hand-written Ethernet/IPv4/IPv6/UDP layer with ARP and NDP. Applications keep picoquic's context and stream-callback API, but instead of the socket loop they call picoquic_packet_loop_dpdk(), which needs a DPDK port, queue ID, mbuf mempool, TX buffer and MAC addresses. It ships mainly as a demo binary (dpdk_picoquicdemo, launched with --dpdk plus EAL arguments) that includes a multi-core server sharded by RSS. This IPNetworkingLab repo is the May-June 2022 thesis snapshot. The CoNEXT-SW '22 paper cites UCLouvain-ENSG/picoquic-dpdk, a later copy from October 2022 with the same core loop.
how_it_is_fast: Kernel bypass with DPDK. It busy-polls the NIC with rte_eth_rx_burst, so there are no interrupts, no syscalls, no sk_buff and no user/kernel copy. Packets move in batches: the paper receives up to 32 per burst, and the -@/-* flags set RX and TX batch sizes. picoquic writes each outgoing QUIC packet straight into the mbuf at the UDP-payload offset, headers are copied in front, and packets are queued with rte_eth_tx_buffer and flushed together. The paper's profile shows server I/O falling from 18.7% to 5.7% of CPU cycles, which leaves those cycles for crypto and protocol work.
when_to_use: Lab or research testbed with a dedicated DPDK-capable NIC (the paper used 100 GbE between two Xeon Silver 4314 hosts) where you want one core to push one QUIC connection well past 10 Gbps.
Bulk single-connection downloads measured by goodput: the paper's 20 GB AES-128-GCM transfer reached roughly 15-16 Gbps on 1 core (read from Fig. 1), against about 5 Gbps for kernel-socket picoquic.
Handshake-rate experiments: up to 6000 zero-byte requests/s, about double stock picoquic in the paper.
You already have picoquic-based C code and want to measure how much of your cost is kernel I/O rather than crypto or protocol processing.
Multi-core server scale-out through RSS sharding (one picoquic context per lcore and queue), as long as you do not need connection migration or multipath.
when_not_to_use: Production or internet-facing services: abandoned since 2022, built on what the maintainer calls 'some random base git commit' of picoquic, and missing years of upstream fixes.

Anything without dedicated NIC access. The maintainer says it cannot run locally or without a real device, and it needs root, hugepages and a busy-polling core; a VM without SR-IOV or passthrough will not work.
Apps that need connection migration or multipath on the multi-threaded server; the README says the sharded mode does not support either.
You need numbers that others have reproduced. Jaeger et al. (IFIP Networking 2023) could not reach the reported picoquic goodput and could not easily reproduce the optimizations.
Throughput with 2 cores on kernel TCP is acceptable: in the same figure, picoTLS over kernel TCP with a 2-core pipeline reached about 20 Gbps, above picoquic-dpdk's 1-core result.

integration.dependencies: DPDK (libdpdk via pkg-config), picotls (a matching commit; a later ENSG commit says the picotls API changed), OpenSSL, pthreads
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 2.8.11+; C11/gnu99 GCC or Clang; CMakeLists hard-codes -O3 -march=native -msse4
integration.platforms: Linux with a DPDK-supported NIC; x86-64 as shipped (-msse4 in default flags); has #if branches for DPDK versions before and after 21.11
integration.thread_safety: One picoquic context per DPDK lcore and RX/TX queue, sharded by RSS or rte_flow (-r); no shared state between cores is documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the picoquic connection/stream callback API is unchanged, but the packet loop is replaced by picoquic_packet_loop_dpdk(), which needs DPDK EAL setup, port/queue/mempool/tx_buffer arguments and peer MAC handling

gotchas: The built-in L2/L3 layer is minimal. It learns peer MACs from incoming packets into a fixed table (20 entries in this repo, 256 in the ENSG copy), ignores ICMPv4, and makes the client pass the server MAC with -A.

Unit tests are not maintained. The maintainer said in October 2025 that they never ran the test suite, and an Ubuntu 24.04 / DPDK 21.11.9 report shows many picoquic_ct failures and a segfault in the non-DPDK demo client.
The no-encryption (memcpy AEAD) variant used in the thesis measurements is not in either repo. It was a local patch to picotls aead_encrypt/aead_decrypt.
TX-ring overflow only prints 'PACKET DROPPED!' from the drop callback, and the RX loop polls forever, so each worker core sits at 100% even when idle.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over upstream picoquic only when you control a DPDK NIC and need single-core goodput; upstream is maintained and uses kernel sockets. Against the tumi8 kernel-bypass forks (LSQUIC-DPDK, quiche-DPDK), pick this one if your code is already on picoquic's C API or you need its RSS-sharded multi-core server. Their results come from a different 10G testbed, so the numbers cannot be compared directly.
verified_claims_summary: In the CoNEXT-SW '22 paper, one QUIC connection downloads 20 GB with AES-128-GCM between two Xeon Silver 4314 @ 2.4 GHz hosts over a 100 Gbps link. On one core, picoquic-dpdk reached about 15.7 Gbps (read from Fig. 1) versus about 4.8 Gbps for kernel-socket picoquic, which is roughly the paper's stated 3x. It also beat quicly, msquic (10.6 Gbps with a 3-core pipeline) and quiche, and handled about 2x picoquic's handshake rate. The paper names no compiler; the repo's CMakeLists builds with -O3 -march=native.
status_note: Abandoned research code: this repo was last pushed 2022-06-01 and the paper-cited ENSG copy 2022-10-31. It is MIT-licensed, but you get it as a patched picoquic tree tied to 2022-era DPDK and picotls, not as a reusable library.
